There are two ways to lose credibility with a number, and only one of them ever gets pointed out to you. The first is overstating. You give a figure you cannot deliver, somebody holds you to it, and everyone remembers. That one is loud, it is embarrassing, and it is survivable, because you can see it happening. The second is quieter and far more expensive. You hedge everything. Every figure comes with three conditions, nothing is ever final, and after a year people stop asking you for numbers at all. Nobody will ever tell you this is happening. They will simply route the question to somebody who answers it. What good executives do is neither. They are precise about the degree. This I will stand behind. This is our working assumption. This is indicative and I would not quote it. Three sentences, three different levels of certainty, and every one of them defensible.

The thing nobody warns you about is that a hedge does not travel. In my own language I had thirty years of practice at sounding exactly as certain as I was. In English I had two settings: sure, and sorry. So I would either give a flat number, which was more than I meant, or I would apologise my way around it, which was less. Both were misread. The flat number became a commitment. The apology became doubt about the underlying business, when the only doubt I had was about the decimal. What fixed it was small. I stopped improvising the certainty and started choosing the phrase before the call. It appears that. On the evidence we have. This is provisional. Four or five phrases, used deliberately, and suddenly the room could hear the difference between a number I was guessing at and a number I would defend.

The retention figure is eighty-four percent, and that is a number I will stand behind. On the industrial book, our working assumption is six percent. On the evidence we have, capacity would appear to be tightening. A harder market in twenty twenty-seven is plausible, and it is not yet a forecast.
